title: With Some Help, You Can Find Your Fatal Flaws During Practice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay opens with Tom Brady's practice of paying practice-squad players for intercepting him -- a deliberate incentive to surface his own flaws before they could cost him in a real game -- and generalizes it into a broader principle about proactively stress-testing performance before it matters. It notes that finding fatal flaws is harder outside sports, where the equivalent is asking colleagues or mentors to serve as harsh critics, and identifies the real obstacle: people who ask for tough feedback often react defensively when they get it, which discourages future candor. The essay's resolution is that performers who want to be great must actively reward honesty -- thanking critics and treating their criticism as a genuine contributor to success -- rather than merely tolerating it.
points: Tom Brady paid practice-squad players for intercepting him, creating a high-stakes incentive to expose his own flaws before games mattered.
Top performers proactively stress-test their work -- presentations, pitches, models -- through rehearsal and walk-throughs, looking for repeatable failure patterns.
Outside of sports, the equivalent tool is asking colleagues or mentors to serve as harsh, honest critics.
A common failure mode: people who ask for sharp criticism often react defensively when they receive it, discouraging future candor.
The fix is to actively reward honesty -- thanking critics and crediting their feedback as a real contributor to success, not just tolerating it.
quotes: Tom Brady was renowned in the NFL for paying practice squad players if they intercepted him.
By creating a high-stakes reward during practice, Brady was able to identify and correct any major flaws he had before performing on the real stage.
Fatal flaws come with a host of colorful metaphors to describe the weakness they portend.
Asking colleagues and mentors to serve as harsh critics is more typical for finding flaws in intellectual performance.
When performers plead for sharp criticism but fail to respond favorably to it, they suffocate the likelihood of more critical feedback in the future.
Only performers who strive to be the best can handle and reward such honesty. The question is: How good do you really want to be?
